hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-01.title: Right triangle
hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-01.body:
$9^2+40^2=81+1600=1681=41^2$, so the triangle is right-angled with legs $9$ and $40$. Area $=\frac12\cdot9\cdot40=180$.

**Answer: 180**

hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-02.title: Height is at most $CM$
hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-02.body:
Let $h$ be the distance from $C$ to line $AB$. Since $CM$ joins $C$ to a point of $AB$, $h\le CM=8$. So the area is $\frac12\cdot AB\cdot h\le\frac12\cdot17\cdot8=68$, with equality when $CM\perp AB$.

**Answer: 68**

hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-03.title: Two configurations
hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-03.body:
By the Pythagorean theorem, $HF=\sqrt{35^2-21^2}=28$ and $HE=\sqrt{60^2-21^2}=9\sqrt{39}$. Since $HE>HF$, the point $H$ is either between $E$ and $F$ (so $EF=HE+HF$) or outside segment $EF$ beyond $F$ (so $EF=HE-HF$). The areas are $\frac12\cdot21\cdot EF$, so the difference is $\frac12\cdot21\cdot\big[(HE+HF)-(HE-HF)\big]=\frac12\cdot21\cdot56=588$.

**Answer: 588**

hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-04.title: Tangent lengths
hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-04.body:
Let the other leg be $x$. For a right triangle with legs $a,b$ and inradius $r$, the hypotenuse is $a+b-2r$. So the hypotenuse is $x+3-\frac34=x+\frac94$, and the semiperimeter is $s=\frac{3+x+x+\frac94}{2}=x+\frac{21}{8}$. The area equals $rs=\frac38\left(x+\frac{21}{8}\right)$ and also $\frac{3x}{2}$. Setting these equal: $\frac{3x}{2}=\frac{3x}{8}+\frac{63}{64}$, so $\frac{9x}{8}=\frac{63}{64}$ and $x=\frac78$. The area is $\frac{3}{2}\cdot\frac78=\frac{21}{16}$.

Check: legs $3,\frac78$ give hypotenuse $\sqrt{9+\frac{49}{64}}=\frac{25}{8}$, and $3+\frac78-\frac34=\frac{25}{8}$.

**Answer: $\frac{21}{16}$**

hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-05.title: Sides from the area
hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-05.body:
Let the area be $K$. The sides are $\frac{2K}{15},\frac{2K}{21},\frac{2K}{35}$, which are proportional to $\frac1{15}:\frac1{21}:\frac1{35}=7:5:3$. So the sides are $3k,5k,7k$. By the law of cosines, the angle between sides $3k$ and $5k$ is opposite $7k$: $\cos\theta=\frac{9+25-49}{30}=-\frac12$, so $\theta=120^\circ$. The area is $\frac12(3k)(5k)\sin120^\circ=\frac{15\sqrt3}{4}k^2$. The altitude onto the side $3k$ is the longest one, $35$, so also $K=\frac12(3k)(35)=\frac{105k}{2}$. Setting equal: $\frac{15\sqrt3}{4}k^2=\frac{105}{2}k$, so $k=\frac{14}{\sqrt3}=\frac{14\sqrt3}{3}$ and $K=\frac{105}{2}\cdot\frac{14\sqrt3}{3}=245\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $245\sqrt3$**

hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-06.title: Exclude the long diagonal
hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-06.body:
A bishop checks the king exactly when it is on the same diagonal. The diagonal through the corner has $6$ squares, one of which holds the king, so $5$ squares are bad. There are $35-5=30$ good squares.

**Answer: 30**

hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-07.title: Split by the long diagonal
hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-07.body:
Both kings lie on the main diagonal. A bishop on that diagonal checks the king of the opposite color unless the path is blocked by the other bishop. A white bishop on the diagonal checks the black king unless the black bishop stands between them on the diagonal; likewise the black bishop checks the white king unless the white bishop is between. So either both bishops are on the diagonal, or neither is.

- Both on the diagonal: number the diagonal squares $1,\dots,6$ with the black king on $1$ and the white king on $6$. The white bishop at $a$ checks the black king unless the black bishop at $b$ satisfies $b<a$, and the black bishop checks the white king unless $a>b$ too. So the condition is $b<a$, which holds for exactly one of the two assignments to each of the $\binom42=6$ pairs of squares: $6$ ways.
- Neither on the diagonal: any two distinct off-diagonal squares work: $30\cdot29=870$ ways.

Total $870+6=876$. (A brute-force check over all placements confirms this.)

**Answer: 876**

hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-08.title: Rows and columns must be color-pure
hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-08.body:
If a row contains both colors, then somewhere along it a white and a black rook are adjacent (nothing between them), and they attack each other. So no row or column may contain both colors. Conversely, if the rows and columns used by white rooks are disjoint from those used by black rooks, there is no attack.

So place the white rooks first. If they use $r$ rows and $c$ columns, the black rooks must go in the remaining $(6-r)(6-c)$ squares: $\binom{(6-r)(6-c)}{3}$ ways. The numbers of white placements by $(r,c)$ (a triple of squares occupying $r$ distinct rows and $c$ distinct columns):

| $(r,c)$ | white placements | black placements | product |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(1,3)$ | $120$ | $\binom{15}{3}=455$ | $54600$ |
| $(3,1)$ | $120$ | $455$ | $54600$ |
| $(2,2)$ | $900$ | $\binom{16}{3}=560$ | $504000$ |
| $(2,3)$ | $1800$ | $\binom{12}{3}=220$ | $396000$ |
| $(3,2)$ | $1800$ | $220$ | $396000$ |
| $(3,3)$ | $2400$ | $\binom{9}{3}=84$ | $201600$ |

The total is $54600+54600+504000+396000+396000+201600=1606800$.

**Answer: 1606800**

hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-09.title: Linearity of expectation
hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-09.body:
There are $3\cdot3=9$ knight-king pairs. For one fixed pair, the knight and king occupy a uniformly random ordered pair of distinct squares, $16\cdot15=240$ possibilities. Count those with the knight giving check: for each king square, the number of squares a knight move away is $2$ at a corner ($4$ corners), $3$ at the non-corner edge squares ($8$ of them), and $4$ at the central squares ($4$ of them). That gives $4\cdot2+8\cdot3+4\cdot4=48$ checking positions, so each pair gives a check with probability $\frac{48}{240}=\frac15$. By linearity of expectation the expected number of checks is $9\cdot\frac15=\frac95$.

**Answer: $\frac95$**

hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-10.title: Coloring and a tiling argument
hmmt-nov-2008-gen2-10.body:
Color the board like a checkerboard ($18$ squares of each color). Each domino covers one square of each color, so the two removed squares must have different colors; otherwise a tiling is impossible.

Conversely, take a Hamiltonian cycle of the board squares, (for example: along row $1$ from column $1$ to column $6$; then snake through columns $2$-$6$ of rows $2,\dots,6$, going right-to-left in row $2$, left-to-right in row $3$, and so on, finishing in row $6$ at column $2$; then return up column $1$ from row $6$ to row $2$ and close the cycle at the starting square). Consecutive squares on it have opposite colors, so the positions along the cycle alternate in color. If the two knights have opposite colors, they sit at positions an odd distance apart on the cycle, so removing them cuts the cycle into two paths, each with an even number of squares. Each path can be tiled by dominoes (pair up consecutive squares). So every opposite-color pair works.

Hence the arrangements that work are exactly the pairs of opposite-colored squares: $18\cdot18=324$.

**Answer: 324**
